24698.q: When was winter grain such as rye sown?
24698.e: Winter grain was sown in autumn. It sprouted before winter and carried on growing the next spring.
24698.m: Winter grain was sown in autumn.

24699.q: When did farmers often slaughter their pigs?
24699.e: There was little animal feed in winter. So pigs were slaughtered in late autumn and supplies were made.
24699.m: Pigs were often slaughtered in late autumn.

24700.q: What did the pigs eat in the forest in autumn?
24700.e: Farmers drove their pigs into the forest in autumn. There they ate acorns and beechnuts and grew fat.
24700.m: In autumn, pigs ate acorns in the forest.

24701.q: What did farmers make from grass in summer as winter feed?
24701.e: Mown grass was left to dry in the sun. This made hay, the feed for winter.

24702.e: Grapes ripen in autumn. The grape harvest is called the vintage.

24703.q: What did farmers often do in winter?
24703.e: In winter there was no work in the fields. People chopped wood, mended tools, spun and wove.
24703.m: In winter, farmers mended their tools.

24704.q: Where did farmers in the Swiss mountains take their cattle in summer?
24704.e: In summer, lots of grass grew high up in the mountains. So the cattle were driven up to the alpine pastures.
24704.m: In summer, the cattle went up to the alpine pastures.

24705.q: On which feast day in November did farmers often have to bring their dues?
24705.e: St Martin's Day on 11 November was an important day for paying dues. In Sursee people still celebrate the Gansabhauet on this day.
24705.m: On St Martin's Day, farmers often brought their dues.

24706.q: What did farmers base their work during the year on?
a: The ringing of the town bell
24706.e: Sowing, harvesting and resting depended on the weather and the seasons.
24706.m: The farmers' work followed the seasons.

24707.q: Which tree often stood in the middle of the village?
24707.e: In many villages a big lime tree stood on the village square. It is called the village lime.
24707.m: Many villages had a village lime tree.

24708.q: What did people in the village do under the village lime tree?
24708.e: The village lime was a meeting place. People talked, celebrated and swapped news there.
24708.m: People met under the village lime tree.

24709.q: What was sometimes held under a lime tree?
24709.e: Court was held under some lime trees. They are called court limes.
24709.m: Court was held under a court lime.

24710.q: What do you call a lime tree that people danced under?
24710.e: People danced under some lime trees at festivals. That is why they are called dance limes.
24710.m: People danced under a dance lime.

24711.q: What shape are the leaves of the lime tree?
24711.e: Lime leaves look like a heart. That makes the lime tree easy to recognise.
24711.m: Lime leaves are shaped like a heart.

24712.q: What can you make from lime blossoms?
24712.e: Lime blossoms smell sweet. They are dried and made into tea.
24712.m: Lime blossoms are made into tea.

24713.q: How old can lime trees get?
24713.e: Lime trees grow slowly and can get very old, sometimes even over a thousand years.
24713.m: Lime trees can live for several hundred years.

24714.q: In which canton is the famous old lime tree of Linn?
24714.e: The lime tree of Linn stands on the Bözberg in the canton of Aargau. It is one of the best-known lime trees in Switzerland.
24714.m: The lime tree of Linn is in the canton of Aargau.

24715.q: Which animal did wool usually come from?
24715.e: Sheep have a thick coat. Wool is obtained from it.

24716.q: How do you get the wool from a sheep?
24716.e: The sheep's coat is cut off. This is called shearing, and it does not hurt the sheep.

24717.q: What do you call the work of twisting wool into a thread?
24717.e: When spinning, you twist the wool fibres into a long thread.

24718.q: Which simple tool was turned when spinning?
24718.e: The spindle is a wooden stick with a weight. When it spins, the wool becomes thread.
24718.m: A spindle was turned for spinning.

24719.q: On which device was cloth made from threads?
24719.e: On the loom, threads are crossed over each other. That makes a piece of cloth.
24719.m: Cloth is woven on a loom.

24720.q: What colours were farmers' clothes usually?
24720.e: Bright colours were expensive. Farmers mostly wore cloth in natural colours such as brown and grey.
24720.m: Farmers' clothes were usually brown or grey.

24721.q: What did farmers often wear in the Middle Ages?
24721.e: A tunic is a long, simple shirt. A belt was often tied over it.
24721.m: Farmers often wore a simple tunic.

24722.q: Why were woollen clothes good in winter?
24722.e: Wool holds in warmth well. That is why you feel less cold in woollen clothes.
24722.m: Wool keeps you warm in winter.

24723.q: What was cloth dyed with in the Middle Ages?
24723.e: Dyes were made from leaves, roots and flowers, for example red from madder.
24723.m: Cloth was dyed with colours from plants.

24724.q: Why was a wall built round a town in the Middle Ages?
24724.e: The thick town wall kept enemies and robbers out. Only those who came through the guarded entrances got into the town.
24724.m: The town wall protected people from enemies.

24725.q: What is the water-filled ditch in front of some town walls called?
24725.e: In front of many walls there was a deep ditch, often filled with water. That made it harder for attackers to reach the wall.
24725.m: The town moat made the wall even safer.

24726.q: In which Swiss town can you still walk a long way along the old town wall today?
24726.e: The town wall of Murten is very well preserved. You can walk a long way round the old town on its covered walkway.
24726.m: In Murten you can walk along the old town wall.

24727.q: What is the long wall with nine towers in Lucerne called?
24727.e: The Musegg Wall protected Lucerne in the Middle Ages. It has nine towers, and you can visit some of them in summer.
24727.m: The Musegg Wall in Lucerne has nine towers.

24728.q: What stood at regular intervals along the town wall?
24728.e: From the wall towers, the guards could see far across the land. That way they noticed enemies early.
24728.m: There were many towers on the town wall.

24729.q: How did you get through the town wall into the town?
24729.e: The town wall had only a few openings. People went through the big gates, which were guarded.
24729.m: You entered the town through the town gate.

24730.q: What did merchants often have to pay for their goods at the town gate?
24730.e: Anyone bringing goods into the town had to pay a charge. The town used this money, for example, to pay for its walls.
24730.m: At the town gate you often had to pay a toll on goods.

24731.q: Which well-known old town gate is in Basel?
24731.e: The Spalentor is a large gate of Basel's old town fortifications. It has a colourful tiled roof and can still be seen today.
24731.m: The Spalentor is an old town gate in Basel.

24732.q: What was the Zytglogge in Bern once?
24732.e: The Zytglogge was first a gate in Bern's town wall. Later the tower got a famous clock.
24732.m: The Zytglogge in Bern used to be a town gate.

24733.q: Who kept watch at the town gate over who came into the town?
24733.e: Guards stood at the gate. They checked who wanted to come into the town.
24733.m: The gatekeeper guarded the town gate.

24734.q: Where did merchants and farmers sell their goods in the town?
24734.e: The market square was a large open space. On market day there were many stalls with goods.
24734.m: Trading took place in the market square.

24735.q: What is a market that takes place every week called?
24735.e: On a certain day of the week, farmers came into the town. Many Swiss towns still have this market today.
24735.m: The weekly market takes place every week.

24736.q: What is a large market that takes place only once or a few times a year called?
24736.e: Merchants came from far away to the big yearly market. There was also entertainment and lots to see.
24736.m: A fair takes place only rarely in the year.

24737.q: What did farmers from the countryside bring to the town market?
24737.e: The farmers sold what grew on their farm. Bananas, cocoa, tomatoes and maize were not yet known in Europe in the Middle Ages.
24737.m: Farmers sold vegetables and eggs at the market.

24738.q: What did people pay with at the market in the Middle Ages?
24738.e: Money then came as coins, mostly made of silver. Sometimes people also swapped goods for goods.
24738.m: In the Middle Ages, people paid with coins.

24739.q: What did merchants use to weigh flour or salt?
24739.e: Many goods were sold by weight. The town checked whether the scales and weights were correct.

24740.q: What did a market crier do?
24740.e: A market crier shouted loudly about how good and cheap his goods were. That drew buyers to his stall.
24740.m: The market crier loudly praised his goods.

24741.q: What is mainly sold at the Zibelemärit in Bern?
24741.e: “Zibele” is Bernese German for onion. The market takes place every year in November, and there are onion plaits everywhere.
24741.m: There are lots of onions at the Zibelemärit in Bern.

24742.q: What was the leader of a guild called?
24742.e: The members chose a leader. He led the meetings and represented the guild to the outside world.
24742.m: The guild master led the guild.

24743.q: What were the guilds in Zurich allowed to do from 1336?
a: Have a say in the council
24743.e: In 1336, Mayor Rudolf Brun gave the craftsmen seats on the council. That way the guilds in Zurich could help to govern.
24743.m: From 1336, the guilds in Zurich helped to govern.

24744.q: In which Swiss city do the guilds parade through the streets at Sechseläuten?
24744.e: Sechseläuten is the spring festival of the Zurich guilds. The members parade through the city in old costumes.
24744.m: Sechseläuten is the guild festival in Zurich.

24745.q: What is burned at the end of Zurich's Sechseläuten?
24745.e: The Böögg is a big snowman made of cotton wool and wood. It stands for winter, which is being driven away.
24745.m: The Böögg is burned at Sechseläuten.

24746.q: Which symbol do you often see on the sign of the bakers' guild?
24746.e: Many people could not read in those days. So pictures such as the pretzel showed which craft was at home where.
24746.m: The pretzel is a symbol of bakers.

24747.q: In the Middle Ages, could anyone in the town simply work at a craft?
24747.e: Anyone who wanted to work at a craft had to be accepted into the guild. This is called compulsory guild membership.
24747.m: Without a guild you were not allowed to work at a craft.

24748.q: Who did the guild help when a member had died?
24748.e: Guild members helped each other. When a member died, the guild supported his family.
24748.m: The guild helped its members' families.

24749.q: Who set the rules for good work in a guild?
24749.e: The guild decided how good a product had to be and how much it was allowed to cost. Anyone who did bad work was punished.
24749.m: The guild made sure the work was good.

24751.q: Which order is correct in a craft?
24751.e: First you learn as an apprentice. After the apprenticeship you are a journeyman and can later become a master.
24751.m: An apprentice becomes a journeyman and then a master.

24752.q: Where did an apprentice often live in the Middle Ages?
24752.e: The apprentice lived with the master's family. He got food and a bed there.
24752.m: The apprentice often lived with the master.

24753.q: What did many journeymen do after their apprenticeship?
24753.e: The journeymen went to other towns and worked for other masters. That way they learned new ways of working.
24753.m: Many journeymen travelled from town to town.

24754.q: How long did an apprenticeship usually last in the Middle Ages?
24754.e: You cannot learn a craft quickly. Depending on the trade, an apprenticeship lasted about two to seven years.

24755.q: What did a master often receive for training an apprentice?
24755.e: The parents often paid the master money for the training. In return their child learned a trade.
24755.m: Parents often paid apprentice fees for the apprenticeship.

24756.q: What are the travels of journeymen still called today?
24756.e: In German-speaking countries people say a journeyman is “auf der Walz”, on his journeyman years. Even today some young craftspeople still go travelling like this.
24756.m: Travelling journeymen are on their journeyman years.

24758.q: When did the night watchman make his rounds of the town?
24758.e: When everyone was asleep, the night watchman walked through the lanes. He made sure everything stayed quiet.
24758.m: The night watchman watched over the town at night.

24759.q: What did the night watchman call out in the lanes?
24759.e: Most people had no clock. So the night watchman called out every hour.
24759.m: The night watchman called out the hours.

24760.q: What did the night watchman mainly warn people about?
24760.e: A fire was especially dangerous at night. If the night watchman saw smoke, he woke everyone at once.
24760.m: The night watchman warned about fire.

24761.q: What did the night watchman carry so he could see in the dark?
24761.e: A candle or an oil lamp burned in the lantern. There were no street lamps then.
24761.m: With his lantern the night watchman could see in the dark.

24762.q: What could the night watchman use to raise the alarm loudly?
24762.e: He blew hard into the horn. The loud sound woke the people in their houses.
24762.m: The night watchman raised the alarm with his horn.

24764.q: In which Swiss city does a watchman still call out the hours from the cathedral tower every night?
24764.e: In French the watchman is called “le guet”. Every night from 10 pm to 2 am he calls out the hours from the cathedral tower.
24764.m: In Lausanne the watchman still calls out the hours today.

24765.q: Which weapon did the night watchman often carry?
24765.e: The halberd is a long pole with a spike and an axe blade. The night watchman could defend himself with it.
24765.m: The night watchman often carried a halberd.

24766.q: Who met in the town hall to make decisions about the town?
24766.e: In the town hall, the council discussed the town's affairs. It made rules for all citizens.
24766.m: The town council met in the town hall.

24767.q: What colour is the famous town hall in Basel?
24767.e: Basel Town Hall is a bright red. It is painted with colourful pictures.

24768.q: What were the men who sat on the town council called?
24768.e: The councillors were mostly rich merchants or craftsmen. They were elected for a certain time.
24768.m: The councillors sat on the town council.

24770.q: Which river is Zurich Town Hall on?
24770.e: Zurich Town Hall stands right by the water. It is even partly built into the river.
24770.m: Zurich Town Hall stands on the Limmat.

24771.q: Who led the council in many towns?
24771.e: The mayor was the head of the town. In Bern this office was called Schultheiss.

24772.q: What else took place in the medieval town hall?
24772.e: Disputes and crimes were also decided in the town hall. The council was often also the court.
24772.m: Court was also held in the town hall.

24773.q: Why did towns often build their town hall especially beautifully?
a: So that enemies could not find it
24773.e: A splendid town hall showed that the town was rich and proud. That is why it often has towers, pictures and decorations.
24773.m: A beautiful town hall showed the town's pride.

24774.q: What is the frame of a half-timbered house made of?
24774.e: A half-timbered house has a skeleton of wooden beams. You can see the beams clearly from outside.
24774.m: A half-timbered house has a wooden frame.

24775.q: What were the gaps between the beams often filled with?
24775.e: Twigs were woven between the beams and covered with clay. Later, bricks were often used too.
24775.m: The panels were filled with clay and twigs.

24776.q: What was mixed into the clay to make it hold better?
24776.e: Chopped straw made the clay stronger. That way it cracked less as it dried.

24777.q: Why did the upper floors often stick out further than the floor below?
a: So that rain could get in
24777.e: Space was tight in the crowded town. The overhanging floors gave more room upstairs.

24778.q: What is a half-timbered house often called in Switzerland?
24778.e: In Switzerland the wooden beams are called Riegel. That is why such houses are called Riegelhäuser.
24778.m: In Switzerland, a half-timbered house is often called a Riegelhaus.

24779.q: In which canton can you see especially many half-timbered houses?
24779.e: In eastern Switzerland, especially in Thurgau, there are very many of these houses. In Ticino and Valais people built more with stone.
24779.m: There are many half-timbered houses in Thurgau.

24780.q: Who built the wooden frame of a half-timbered house?
24780.e: The carpenter sawed and joined the beams. He worked with wood, axe and saw.
24780.m: The carpenter built the wooden frame.

24781.q: In which small town are there many painted old houses on the town hall square?
24781.e: The old town of Stein am Rhein is known for its painted façades and half-timbering. It is in the canton of Schaffhausen.
24781.m: Stein am Rhein has many painted old houses.

24782.q: Where did most townspeople get their water from in the Middle Ages?
a: From the water carrier at the market
24782.e: There were no water pipes into the houses yet. People carried the water home in buckets from the fountain.
24782.m: Water was fetched from the fountain.

24783.q: Who often fetched the water from the fountain?
24783.e: Fetching water was a daily chore. Often the maids or the family's children did it.
24783.m: Maids and children often fetched the water.

24784.q: What did people often exchange at the fountain?
24784.e: You met your neighbours at the fountain every day. There people told each other what was happening in the town.
24784.m: The fountain was a meeting place for news.

24785.q: What was fountain water especially important for in an emergency?
24785.e: When a fire broke out, people formed a chain. They passed buckets of water along from the fountain.
24785.m: Fountain water was used to put out fires.

24786.q: Which Swiss city is known for its many painted figure fountains from the 16th century?
24786.e: There are many old fountains with colourful figures in Bern's old town. They are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
24786.m: Bern has many old figure fountains.

24787.q: Which animal in a knight's armour stands on the Zähringen Fountain in Bern?
24787.e: The bear is the heraldic animal of Bern. On this fountain it wears armour and holds a flag.
24787.m: A bear in armour stands on the Zähringen Fountain.

24788.q: What is special about a running fountain?
a: The water flows all the time
You have to pump the water up
You fetch the water with a bucket
24788.e: In a running fountain, the water comes through pipes from a spring. It flows from the spout into the trough day and night.
24788.m: Water flows all the time from a running fountain.

24789.q: What were the troughs of town fountains usually made of?
24789.e: Stone is strong and lasts a long time. That is why many old stone fountains are still standing today.
24789.m: Many old fountains are made of stone.

24790.q: Which city in Norway was an important place of the Hanseatic League?
24790.e: The Hanseatic merchants had a large trading post in Bergen. You can still see the old wooden houses by the harbour today.
24790.m: Bergen in Norway was a Hanseatic town.

24791.q: Which city is called the “Queen of the Hanseatic League”?
24791.e: Lübeck on the Baltic Sea was the most important city of the Hanseatic League. The Hanseatic towns met there for their assemblies.
24791.m: Lübeck was the Queen of the Hanseatic League.

24792.q: Which sea were many Hanseatic towns on?
24792.e: The Hanseatic League traded mainly in northern Europe. Many of its towns were on the Baltic Sea and the North Sea.
24792.m: Many Hanseatic towns were on the Baltic Sea.

24793.q: Which city still calls itself a “Free and Hanseatic City” today?
24793.e: Hamburg was an important Hanseatic town. Its name still reminds people of this today, as do its number plates with “HH”.

24794.q: Which fish did the Hanseatic League trade in especially?
24794.e: Herring was preserved in salt and so it kept for a long time. It was sold to many countries.
24794.m: The Hanseatic League traded a lot of herring.

24795.e: The cog was the typical trading ship of the Hanseatic League. It had a thick, round wooden hull.
24795.m: The cog is an old sailing ship.

24796.q: How many masts did a typical cog have?
24796.e: A cog had one mast with a big square sail. The wind drove it across the sea.

24797.q: In which city was an old cog found in the river in 1962?
24797.e: During building work in the River Weser, an old ship came to light. The Bremen Cog can be seen in a museum today.
24797.m: The Bremen Cog was found in 1962.

24798.q: What were cogs used for in the Middle Ages?
24798.e: Cogs had lots of space in their hold. They carried goods such as salt, grain and cloth from port to port.
24798.m: Cogs were used to transport goods.

24799.q: What did jugglers and entertainers do at the market?
24799.e: Entertainers amused people with tricks and acrobatics. In return they got a few coins.

24800.q: Which trick did travelling entertainers often perform?
24800.e: When juggling, you throw several balls into the air and catch them again. Many entertainers were very good at it.

24801.q: Where did travelling entertainers usually live?
a: They moved from place to place
24801.e: Entertainers had no fixed home. They travelled to markets and festivals in different towns.
24801.m: Entertainers moved from place to place.

24802.q: What did some entertainers balance on high above the square?
24802.e: Tightrope walkers stretched a rope high above the spectators' heads. They walked and danced on it.
24802.m: Tightrope walkers balanced on a rope.

24803.q: What did some entertainers breathe out to amaze people?
24803.e: Fire-breathers blow a flame into the air. This is very dangerous and must not be copied.

24804.q: What did minstrels do in the Middle Ages?
24804.e: Minstrels travelled around and performed at markets, festivals and castles. They sang and made music.

24805.q: Which instrument did minstrels often play?
24805.e: Bagpipes have an air bag and pipes. They are easy to carry when you travel from place to place.

24806.q: Which musical instrument has a crank?
24806.e: On a hurdy-gurdy you turn a crank. A wheel then rubs against the strings.
24806.m: The hurdy-gurdy is played with a crank.

24807.q: What did minstrels often tell about in their songs?
24807.e: Their songs were about brave heroes, love and adventures. People loved listening.
24807.m: Minstrels sang about heroes and adventures.

24808.q: What was the man who ran a bathhouse called?
24808.e: The bath keeper looked after the bath and the hot water. He had other jobs as well.
24808.m: The bath keeper ran the bathhouse.

24809.q: What did people do in the bathhouse?
24809.e: There were no bathrooms in the houses. So people went to the bathhouse to wash.

24810.q: What else did the bath keeper do apart from baths?
24810.e: The bath keeper cut hair and shaved beards. So he was also a kind of hairdresser.
24810.m: The bath keeper also cut hair.

24811.q: What did the bath keeper do when someone had bad toothache?
a: He sent them to the doctor
He filled the hole with gold
He gave them a honey ointment
24811.e: There were no dentists like today. The bath keeper simply pulled out bad teeth.
24811.m: The bath keeper pulled out bad teeth.

24812.q: How was the water in the bathhouse heated?
a: With warm stones from the stream
With warm water from a spring
24812.e: The water was heated in big cauldrons over the fire. That needed a lot of wood.
24812.m: In the bathhouse, water was heated with fire.

24813.q: What did many bathhouses have besides warm water?
24813.e: In the sweat bath, water was poured onto hot stones. This made steam, a bit like a sauna.
24813.m: You could also sweat in the bathhouse.

24814.q: What did people bathe in at the bathhouse?
24814.e: A tub is a big wooden vat. It was filled with warm water, and often several people sat in it.
24814.m: In the bathhouse people bathed in a wooden tub.

24815.q: What did the bath keeper do when cupping?
a: He put warm glasses on the skin
He rubbed the skin with salt
He put leaves on the skin
He wrapped the skin in wet cloths
24815.e: In cupping, small warmed glasses were placed on the back. People believed it helped against illnesses.
24815.m: In cupping, warm glasses were put on the skin.

24816.q: What did a place receive in the Middle Ages when it became a town?
24816.e: With town rights, a place received special rights. Only then was it really a town.
24816.m: Town rights turned a place into a town.

24817.q: Who granted town rights in the Middle Ages?
24817.e: The ruler of the land gave a place its town rights. In return he often got taxes from the town.
24817.m: A king or prince granted town rights.

24818.q: Which right was often part of town rights?
24818.e: Town rights often included the right to hold a market and to build a wall. That way the town became rich and safe.
24818.m: With town rights, a town was often allowed to hold a market.

24819.q: What did the men of a town have to do when there was danger?
24819.e: The town had hardly any soldiers of its own. So the men had to keep watch and defend the wall themselves.
24819.m: The men of the town had to defend it themselves.

24820.q: What was a town that was directly under the king or emperor called?
24820.e: Such a town had no prince above it, only the king. Zurich and Bern were also towns like this.
24820.m: An imperial city was directly under the king.

24821.q: How long did an unfree person have to live in a town to become free?
24821.e: If his lord had not fetched him back in that time, he was free. This rule applied in many towns.
24821.m: After a year and a day in the town, you were free.

24822.q: Which important right did a town often receive together with its town rights?
24822.e: With this right the town was allowed to hold markets regularly. That brought merchants and money into the town.
24822.m: Market rights allowed a town to hold markets.

24823.q: Where were the rules of a town written down?
a: On a wooden board at the fountain
24823.e: The rights of a town were written in a charter with a seal. The citizens kept it safe.
24823.m: The town rights were written in a charter.

24824.q: What is the long robe that monks wear called?
24824.e: Monks wear a long, simple robe with a hood. It is called a habit or cowl.
24824.m: The habit is the simple robe of monks.

24825.q: What did nuns usually wear on their heads?
24825.e: Nuns covered their hair with a veil. It showed that they had given their lives to God.
24825.m: Nuns wear a veil on their heads.

24826.q: What is the shaved circle on the heads of many monks called?
24826.e: Many monks had the hair on top of their heads cut off. This hairstyle is called a tonsure.
24826.m: The tonsure is the special hairstyle of monks.

24827.q: What did monks and nuns promise when they entered the monastery?
24827.e: Monks and nuns promised to live without owning anything. Such a promise is called a vow.
24827.m: Monks and nuns promise to live in poverty.

24828.q: What were monks and nuns not allowed to do?
24828.e: Monks and nuns lived unmarried. They promised not to marry and not to start a family of their own.
24828.m: Monks and nuns do not marry.

24829.q: What is the covered walkway around a courtyard in a monastery called?
24829.e: The cloister surrounds a courtyard. The monks walked, prayed and read there.
24829.m: The cloister is a walkway around the monastery courtyard.

24830.q: What is the dining hall in a monastery called?
24830.e: In the refectory, monks and nuns ate together. Often they kept silent while someone read aloud.
24830.m: Monks eat together in the refectory.

24831.q: What called the monks to prayer several times a day?
24831.e: The monastery bell rang at fixed times. Then all the monks went to church to pray.
24831.m: The monastery bell calls the monks to prayer.

24832.q: What is the head of a convent of nuns called?
24832.e: A convent is led by an abbess. The nuns choose her from their community.

24833.q: What does the word “abba”, which “abbot” comes from, mean?
24833.e: The word abbot comes from “abba”. It means father. The abbot is meant to be like a father to the monks.
24833.m: The abbot is like a father to the monks.

24834.q: Who usually chose the abbot of a monastery?
24834.e: According to the Rule of St Benedict, the monks choose their abbot themselves. He usually stays in office for a long time.
24834.m: The monks choose their abbot themselves.

24835.q: Which staff does an abbot carry as a sign of his office?
24835.e: The abbot's staff is curved at the top like a shepherd's crook. It shows that the abbot leads his monks like a shepherd.
24835.m: The abbot carries a curved staff like a shepherd.

24836.q: What did monks have to be towards the abbot?
24836.e: Monks promised obedience. They followed their abbot's instructions.

24837.q: What is the abbot's deputy called?
24837.e: The prior helps the abbot and stands in for him when he is away.
24837.m: The prior is the abbot's deputy.

24838.q: Who led the Fraumünster in Zurich in the Middle Ages?
24838.e: The Fraumünster was a convent. Its abbess was very powerful and was even allowed to have coins minted in Zurich.
24838.m: The abbess of the Fraumünster was very powerful in Zurich.

24839.q: What was the abbot of St Gallen, who was also a territorial ruler, called?
24839.e: The abbot of St Gallen also ruled over a territory with villages and farmers. That is why he was called prince-abbot.
24839.m: The prince-abbot of St Gallen was both abbot and ruler.

24840.q: What did monks mainly use medicinal herbs for?
24840.e: Monks made teas, ointments and compresses from medicinal herbs. They used them to care for sick people.
24840.m: Medicinal herbs from the monastery garden were used as medicine.

24841.q: Which medicinal herb with soft, grey-green leaves helps with a sore throat?
24841.e: Sage already grew in monastery gardens. Sage tea helps with a sore throat.
24841.m: Sage helps with a sore throat.

24842.q: Which tea did monks often drink for tummy ache?
24842.e: Camomile soothes the tummy. It still grows in many monastery gardens today.
24842.m: Camomile tea helps with tummy ache.

24843.q: Which orange flower was used to make an ointment for wounds?
24843.e: The marigold has orange or yellow flowers. Its ointment helps with small wounds.
24843.m: Marigold ointment helps with small wounds.

24844.q: Which fresh-smelling herb already grew in monastery gardens and is still popular as a tea today?
24844.e: Mint smells fresh and cool. The monk Walafrid Strabo already described it in his poem about his garden.
24844.m: Mint already grew in monastery gardens.

24845.q: Who looked after the plants in the monastery garden in the Middle Ages?
24845.e: The monks worked in the garden themselves. They planted herbs, vegetables and fruit.
24845.m: Monks looked after the monastery garden.

24846.q: What does the famous old Plan of St Gall show?
24846.e: The Plan of St Gall was drawn more than 1200 years ago. It shows a whole monastery with a herb garden, a vegetable garden and an orchard.
24846.m: The Plan of St Gall shows a whole monastery with gardens.

24847.q: Why was the herb garden in the monastery close to the doctor's house?
a: So the medicinal herbs were close at hand
So the garden was protected from rain
So the plants got more sun
So the doctor could sleep there
24847.e: The doctor needed the medicinal herbs for his patients. That is why the herb garden was right next to his house.
24847.m: The herb garden was close to the doctor.

24848.q: Which purple plant with a strong scent often grew in monastery gardens?
24848.e: Lavender has a strong scent and is calming. It was also used against moths in clothes.
24848.m: Lavender smells strong and grows in many monastery gardens.

24849.q: What did the monks write with in the scriptorium?
24849.e: The monks wrote with a bird's feather. They dipped the tip in ink.
24849.m: Monks wrote with a quill and ink.

24850.q: Which animal did quills usually come from?
24850.e: Goose feathers are big and firm. The tip was cut at a slant, and you could write well with it.

24851.q: Which animal skin was parchment often made from?
24851.e: Parchment was made from the skin of calves, sheep or goats. The skin was cleaned, stretched and scraped thin.
24851.m: Parchment is made from animal skin.

24852.q: What did monks use to remove a writing mistake?
24852.e: The monks scraped the ink off the parchment with a small knife. Then they wrote over it again.
24852.m: Monks scraped away mistakes with a knife.

24853.q: When did the monks usually work in the scriptorium?
a: In the middle of the night
24853.e: Candles gave little light and could start fires. So the monks preferred to write in daylight.
24853.m: In the scriptorium, people wrote in daylight.

24854.q: How long could it take to copy a whole Bible?
24854.e: A Bible has a great many pages. A monk often needed more than a year to copy it by hand.
24854.m: Copying a Bible often took over a year.

24855.q: Which plant growth was often used to make ink in the Middle Ages?
24855.e: Oak galls are small balls on oak leaves. Mixed with iron, they make a dark ink that lasts.
24855.m: Dark ink was made from oak galls.

24856.q: How did the monks behave while writing in the scriptorium?
24856.e: It was quiet in the scriptorium. That way the scribes could concentrate well and made fewer mistakes.
24856.m: Work in the scriptorium was done quietly.

24857.q: What were book covers often made of in the Middle Ages?
24857.e: The pages were bound between two wooden boards. Leather was often stretched over them.
24857.m: Medieval books often had wooden covers.

24858.q: What is the large, decorated first letter of a text called?
24858.e: An initial is the first letter of a section. It is large, colourful and often decorated with pictures.
24858.m: The initial is a large, decorated first letter.

24859.q: Which shiny metal was stuck into splendid books?
24859.e: The book painters stuck wafer-thin gold leaf onto the pages. It still shines today.
24859.m: Gold leaf makes old books shine.

24860.q: Which blue stone was used to make a very expensive blue paint?
24860.e: Lapis lazuli came from far away, from what is now Afghanistan. It was ground into a bright blue powder.
24860.m: The expensive blue was made from lapis lazuli.

24861.q: What is a small painted picture in an old book called?
24861.e: The pictures in manuscripts are called miniatures. The word comes from “minium”, a red paint.
24861.m: Small pictures in old books are called miniatures.

24862.q: Where did book painters often paint little animals and tendrils?
a: In the margin of the page
24862.e: In the margins of the pages they painted leaves, tendrils and funny animals. That made the page even more beautiful.
24862.m: Book painters often painted tendrils and animals in the margins.

24863.q: Which famous, splendidly painted book from Ireland is about 1200 years old?
24863.e: The Book of Kells was made around the year 800. It contains the four Gospels and is beautifully painted.
24863.m: The Book of Kells is a splendid book from Ireland.

24864.q: What did book painters make many of their paints from?
24864.e: Paints were made from plants, earths and ground-up stones. They were mixed, for example, with egg white.
24864.m: Paints were made from plants and stones.

24865.q: Why were painted manuscripts so valuable?
a: Lots of work and expensive paints
24865.e: A painted book needed a lot of time, gold and expensive paints. That is why only monasteries, churches and rich people owned such books.

24866.q: What was Hildegard of Bingen's calling?
24866.e: Hildegard lived in a convent even as a child. Later she became a famous nun and abbess.
24866.m: Hildegard of Bingen was a famous nun.

24867.q: In which country did Hildegard of Bingen live?
24867.e: Hildegard lived in what is now Germany. Later she also founded her own convent there.
24867.m: Hildegard of Bingen lived in what is now Germany.

24868.q: In which century did Hildegard of Bingen live?
24868.e: Hildegard was born in 1098 and died in 1179. So she lived in the 12th century.
24868.m: Hildegard of Bingen lived in the 12th century.

24869.q: What is Hildegard of Bingen especially well known for today?
24869.e: Hildegard wrote about plants, animals and stones and how they can help sick people. That is why she is mainly known today as a healer.
24869.m: Hildegard of Bingen wrote a lot about healing.

24870.q: On which river did Hildegard found her own convent?
24870.e: Around 1150, Hildegard founded the Rupertsberg convent near Bingen. Bingen lies on the Rhine.
24870.m: Hildegard's convent was on the Rhine.

24871.q: Besides books, what else did Hildegard of Bingen write?
24871.e: Hildegard wrote and composed many religious songs. Some are still sung today.

24872.q: What are the special images that Hildegard said she saw inside herself called?
24872.e: Hildegard told of special images that she saw inside herself. They are called visions.

24873.q: Which kind of grain did Hildegard of Bingen especially praise?
24873.e: Hildegard wrote that spelt was especially good and easy to digest. That is why spelt is often linked with her today.

24874.q: What did Hildegard of Bingen officially become in 2012?
24874.e: In 2012, Pope Benedict XVI declared Hildegard a saint and a Doctor of the Church.
24874.m: Hildegard of Bingen has officially been a saint since 2012.

24875.q: Who studied at a monastery school in the Middle Ages?
24875.e: Monastery schools were mainly for boys, who often became monks later. In convents, girls learned too.
24875.m: Monastery schools were mainly for boys.

24876.q: What did children at the monastery school write their exercises on?
24876.e: Parchment was too expensive for practising. The children scratched into a wax tablet with a stylus.
24876.m: Children practised on a wax tablet.

24877.q: What did people write on a wax tablet with?
24877.e: The stylus was a pointed stick. With its flat end you could smooth the wax again.
24877.m: People wrote on wax with a stylus.

24878.q: What did the children at the monastery school often practise together?
24878.e: There was a lot of singing in the monastery. The children learned the songs for church services by heart.
24878.m: At the monastery school the children practised singing.

24879.q: Which emperor had schools in monasteries supported around the year 800?
24879.e: Charlemagne wanted more people to be able to read and write. That is why he supported schools in monasteries and at churches.

24880.q: Which monastery school in Switzerland was especially famous in the Middle Ages?
24880.e: The monastery school of St Gallen was one of the best in Europe more than 1000 years ago. Learned monks taught there.
24880.m: The monastery school of St Gallen was very famous.

24881.q: Who taught the children at a monastery school?
24881.e: At the monastery school, learned monks were the teachers. They could read, write and sing.
24881.m: Monks taught at the monastery school.

24882.q: What often happened when a pupil at the monastery school did not pay attention?
a: He was beaten with a rod
He had to muck out the stable
24882.e: Teachers in the Middle Ages were very strict. Anyone who did not pay attention was often beaten with a rod.
24882.m: Teachers at the monastery school were very strict.

24883.q: Who wrote the well-known rule for monks that goes with “Pray and work”?
24883.e: Benedict of Nursia wrote a rule for life in the monastery around the year 540. His monks are called Benedictines.
24883.m: Benedict of Nursia wrote the Benedictine Rule.

24884.q: In which country did Benedict of Nursia live?
24884.e: Benedict was born in Nursia in Italy. He founded the monastery of Monte Cassino.
24884.m: Benedict of Nursia lived in Italy.

24885.q: What is the famous monastery that Benedict founded on a mountain called?
24885.e: Around 529, Benedict founded the monastery of Monte Cassino in Italy. It is on a mountain.
24885.m: Benedict founded the monastery of Monte Cassino.

24886.q: Which work, for example, did monks do following “Pray and work”?
24886.e: The monks worked in the fields, in the garden, in the kitchen or in the writing room. Work was as much a part of the day as prayer.
24886.m: In the monastery, praying and working go together.

24887.q: How often a day did the monks pray together?
24887.e: The monks met several times a day to pray, early in the morning and even at night. In between they worked.
24887.m: Monks pray together several times a day.

24888.q: According to the rule, why should monks work?
24888.e: Benedict wrote that idleness is an enemy of the soul. That is why the monks were to work every day.

24889.q: What are the monks who live by the Rule of St Benedict called?
24889.e: Anyone who lives by Benedict's rule is a Benedictine. There are still Benedictines in Switzerland today.
24889.m: Benedictines live by the Rule of St Benedict.

24890.q: Which Benedictine monastery is in the canton of Obwalden?
24890.e: Engelberg Abbey was founded in 1120. Benedictines still live there today by the motto “Pray and work”.

24891.q: What are people who walk to a holy place called?
24891.e: Pilgrims walk to a holy place to pray. Many pilgrims were already on the road in the Middle Ages.
24891.m: Pilgrims walk to a holy place.

24892.q: In which city does the Way of St James end?
24892.e: The Way of St James leads to Santiago de Compostela. The apostle James is said to be buried there.
24892.m: The Way of St James leads to Santiago de Compostela.

24893.q: In which country is Santiago de Compostela?
24893.e: Santiago de Compostela is in north-west Spain, in the region of Galicia.
24893.m: Santiago de Compostela is in Spain.

24894.q: Which symbol do pilgrims on the Way of St James wear?
24894.e: The scallop shell is the symbol of the pilgrims of St James. You can also see it on the signposts.
24894.m: The shell is the symbol of the pilgrims of St James.

24895.q: What do pilgrims on the Way of St James mainly do?
24895.e: Pilgrims walk the Way of St James on foot, step by step. The route is named after the apostle James.
24895.m: On the Way of St James, pilgrims walk.

24896.q: How did most pilgrims travel in the Middle Ages?
24896.e: Most pilgrims walked. The journey often took many months.
24896.m: Pilgrims in the Middle Ages mostly went on foot.

24897.q: What did pilgrims take with them for support on their walk?
24897.e: The pilgrim's staff helped with walking and for keeping dogs away. Every pilgrim had one.
24897.m: Pilgrims walk with a pilgrim's staff.

24898.q: In which Swiss city does the Way of St James leave Switzerland towards France?
24898.e: The Way of St James runs right across Switzerland to Geneva. From there it continues through France to Spain.
24898.m: The Swiss Way of St James leads to Geneva.

24899.q: What do pilgrims today have stamped in their pilgrim passport along the way?
24899.e: Pilgrims get a stamp in churches and places to stay. That shows everywhere they have been.
24899.m: Pilgrims collect stamps of their stops in the pilgrim passport.

24900.q: What shape are the arches in Gothic churches?
24900.e: Gothic churches have pointed arches over windows and doors. They point up towards the sky.

24901.q: How are Gothic churches usually built?
24901.e: The builders of the Gothic period wanted to build as tall as possible. Lots of light came into the church through big windows.
24901.m: Gothic churches are tall and bright.

24902.q: In which country did the Gothic style of building begin?
24902.e: Gothic began around 1140 in France, near Paris. From there it spread all over Europe.

24903.q: What are the stone figures on churches with rainwater running out of their mouths called?
24903.e: Gargoyles carry rainwater away from the church wall. They often look like monsters or animals.
24903.m: Gargoyles carry rainwater away from the roof.

24904.q: Which Gothic church in Bern has the tallest church tower in Switzerland?
24904.e: The tower of Bern Minster is about 100 metres tall. It is the tallest church tower in Switzerland.
24904.m: Bern Minster has the tallest church tower in Switzerland.

24905.q: Which large Gothic cathedral stands in Lausanne?
24905.e: Lausanne Cathedral was solemnly consecrated in 1275. It is considered the most important Gothic building in Switzerland.
24905.m: There is a large Gothic cathedral in Lausanne.

24906.q: What are the supports on the outside of Gothic churches that hold up the tall walls called?
24906.e: Flying buttresses support the walls from outside. That made it possible to build higher and fit bigger windows.
24906.m: Flying buttresses support Gothic churches from outside.

24907.q: Which famous Gothic church in Germany has two very tall towers?
24907.e: Cologne Cathedral is a Gothic cathedral with two towers over 150 metres tall. It was only finished in 1880.
24907.m: Cologne Cathedral is a famous Gothic church.

24908.q: In which city is Notre-Dame Cathedral, which caught fire in 2019?
24908.e: Notre-Dame Cathedral is in Paris. In April 2019 its roof burned.

24909.e: “Notre-Dame” means Mary, the mother of Jesus. In English we say “Our Lady”.

24910.q: In which city is the famous church of Notre-Dame?
24910.e: Notre-Dame is a large, old church in Paris. It was built in the Middle Ages.

24911.q: Which river is Notre-Dame de Paris on?
24911.e: The Seine flows right through Paris. The cathedral stands on an island in this river.

24912.q: Roughly when did building work on Notre-Dame in Paris begin?
24912.e: Building began in 1163. It took almost 200 years until the cathedral was finished.

24913.q: What collapsed in the Notre-Dame fire in 2019?
a: The bridge in front of it
24913.e: In the fire, the slender spire above the roof collapsed. The two big main towers stayed standing.
24913.m: In the 2019 fire, the pointed spire of Notre-Dame collapsed.

24914.q: In which year did Notre-Dame reopen after the fire?
24914.e: After more than five years of work, Notre-Dame reopened in December 2024.

24915.q: What is the name of the bell-ringer of Notre-Dame in Victor Hugo's famous story?
24915.e: Victor Hugo wrote a novel about Notre-Dame in 1831. In it, Quasimodo rings the bells of the cathedral.
24915.m: Quasimodo is the bell-ringer of Notre-Dame.

24916.q: What are the colourful pictures in church windows made of?
24916.e: Lots of small pieces of coloured glass are put together. When the sun shines, they glow.
24916.m: Church windows are made of many pieces of coloured glass.

24917.q: Which metal held the pieces of glass in church windows together?
24917.e: The pieces of glass were joined with narrow strips of lead. That is why they are also called leaded glass windows.
24917.m: Strips of lead hold the pieces of glass in the window together.

24918.q: Why did church windows often show stories from the Bible?
24918.e: Most people in the Middle Ages could not read. The pictures in the windows told them the stories of the Bible.
24918.m: Church windows told Bible stories in pictures.

24919.q: What is a large, round church window that looks like a flower called?
24919.e: The rose window is a round window with many parts. It looks like a rose.
24919.m: A round church window like a flower is called a rose window.

24920.q: When do church windows glow most beautifully inside the church?
24920.e: Sunlight falls through the coloured glass. Then the colours glow inside the church.
24920.m: Church windows glow when the sun shines through them.

24921.q: What happens when the sun shines through a piece of coloured glass?
24921.e: Coloured glass only lets its own colour through. That is why sunlight paints coloured patches on the floor and walls of the church.

24922.q: In which building are there often windows of coloured glass?
24922.e: Many churches have stained glass windows. They often show pictures from the Bible.
24922.m: Churches often have stained glass windows.

24923.q: How was glass for church windows coloured in the Middle Ages?
24923.e: Metals such as copper or cobalt were mixed into the liquid glass. That made it green, red or blue.

24924.q: Which people did Charlemagne rule as king?
24924.e: Charlemagne was King of the Franks. In the Middle Ages their kingdom was the largest in Western Europe.
24924.m: Charlemagne was King of the Franks.

24925.q: Which people did Charlemagne fight against for many years?
24925.e: Charlemagne waged war for more than 30 years against the Saxons in the north. In the end they became part of his empire.
24925.m: Charlemagne fought the Saxons for a long time.

24926.q: Roughly how long did Charlemagne reign?
24926.e: Charlemagne became king in 768 and died in 814. So he reigned for 46 years.
24926.m: Charlemagne reigned for a very long time.

a: In St Peter's Basilica in Rome
24927.e: Charlemagne died in Aachen in 814. He was buried in his church, today's Aachen Cathedral.

24928.q: What is Charlemagne's ruling family called?
24928.e: The name comes from “Charles”, in Latin “Carolus”. Several important rulers of this family were called Charles.

24929.q: Which monastery in the Grisons is said to have been founded by Charlemagne?
24929.e: According to tradition, Charlemagne had the Convent of St John in Müstair built. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
24929.m: Müstair Abbey is said to go back to Charlemagne.

24930.q: Which big animal did Charlemagne receive as a present from Baghdad?
24930.e: The caliph Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne an elephant. It was called Abul Abbas.

24931.q: What is Charles the Great called in French?
24931.e: In French, Charles the Great is called “Charlemagne”. That also means “Charles the Great”.
24931.m: In French, Charles the Great is called Charlemagne.

24932.q: What did Charlemagne have set up at monasteries and churches?
24932.e: Charlemagne wanted more people to learn to read and write. That is why he supported schools at monasteries and churches.

24933.q: What does a king wear on his head?
24933.e: The crown is a king's most important symbol. He wears it on his head.
24933.m: The king wears the crown on his head.

24934.e: The sceptre is a decorated staff. The king holds it in his hand as a sign of his power.
24934.m: The sceptre is the ruler's staff.

24935.q: What is the golden ball with a cross that an emperor holds in his hand called?
24935.e: The ball with the cross is called an orb. It stands for the world that the ruler governs.
24935.m: The orb is a ball with a cross.

24936.q: What were kings' crowns usually made of?
24936.e: Crowns were made of gold and decorated with precious stones and pearls. That way they showed wealth and power.
24936.m: Crowns were made of gold and decorated with precious stones.

24937.q: Which special chair does a king sit on?
24937.e: The throne is the ruler's seat of honour. It is often raised so that everyone looks up to the king.
24937.m: The king sits on a throne.

24938.q: In which city can you see the Imperial Crown of the German emperors today?
24938.e: The old Imperial Crown is kept in the treasury in Vienna. It is about 1000 years old.
24938.m: The Imperial Crown is in Vienna today.

24939.q: How many corners does the old Imperial Crown have?
24939.e: The Imperial Crown is made of eight gold plates. That is why it has eight corners.
24939.m: The Imperial Crown has eight corners.

24940.q: What did the crown and sceptre show everyone?
a: What the weather will be like
24940.e: Crown and sceptre are called symbols of rule. You could recognise the king or emperor by them straight away.
24940.m: Crown and sceptre show who rules.

24941.q: Who crowned the emperor in the Middle Ages?
24941.e: The Pope placed the crown on the emperor's head in Rome. This showed that the emperor was also recognised by the Church.

24942.q: In which city were emperors usually crowned in the Middle Ages?
24942.e: The imperial coronation took place in Rome. That is where the Pope lived.

24943.q: On which feast day was Charlemagne crowned emperor?
24943.e: Charlemagne was crowned on 25 December in the year 800. That is Christmas Day.
24943.m: Charlemagne became emperor on Christmas Day.

24944.q: In which church in Rome was Charlemagne crowned?
24944.e: Charlemagne was crowned in the old St Peter's in Rome. Today's St Peter's Basilica stands in its place.
24944.m: Charlemagne was crowned in St Peter's.

24945.q: Who was above a king in the Middle Ages?
24945.e: The emperor was the highest worldly ruler. He was above the kings.
24945.m: The emperor was above the kings.

24946.q: In which city were German kings crowned for a long time before becoming emperor?
24946.e: For many hundreds of years, German kings were crowned in Aachen Cathedral. Charlemagne's throne is there too.
24946.m: German kings were crowned in Aachen.

24947.q: Besides the crown, what did a ruler receive at the coronation?
24947.e: Crown, sceptre and orb are the symbols of power. They are called the imperial regalia.
24947.m: Crown, sceptre and orb show the emperor's power.

24948.q: What was a ruler anointed with at the coronation?
24948.e: At the coronation the ruler was anointed with holy oil. This was meant to show that God had chosen him to rule.
24948.m: At the coronation the ruler was anointed with oil.

a: A residence for the travelling king
24949.e: A Pfalz was a large house where the king lived with his court when he travelled through.
24949.m: The travelling king stayed in the Pfalz.

24950.q: Why did the king need several palaces?
a: He was always travelling through his kingdom
24950.e: In the Middle Ages the king had no fixed capital. He moved from palace to palace and ruled on the move.
24950.m: The king travelled from palace to palace.

24951.q: On which hill in Zurich did a royal palace once stand?
24951.e: In the Middle Ages a royal palace stood on the Lindenhof. Kings stayed here when they came to Zurich.
24951.m: A royal palace stood on the Lindenhof in Zurich.

24952.q: What was there almost always in a royal palace?
24952.e: Every royal palace had a church or chapel. The king prayed there with his people.
24952.m: A royal palace had a chapel.

24953.q: What was the great hall in a royal palace, where the king received guests, called?
24953.e: In the great hall the king held feasts and assemblies. Here he received important guests.
24953.m: The king received his guests in the royal hall.

24954.q: What did the farmers around a royal palace have to supply when the king came?
24954.e: The king came with many people. The farms nearby had to supply bread, meat and other food.
24954.m: The farmers supplied food for the royal court.

24955.q: In which city did Charlemagne have his most important palace?
24955.e: Charlemagne often lived in his palace in Aachen. His palace chapel, part of the cathedral, still stands there today.
24955.m: Charlemagne's most important palace was in Aachen.

24956.q: Which Latin word does the German word “Pfalz” (royal palace) come from?
24956.e: The word Pfalz comes from the Latin “palatium”. The word palace comes from it too.
24956.m: Pfalz and palace come from the same word.

24957.q: Where did the vassal put his hands when swearing his oath of loyalty?
24957.e: The vassal knelt down and placed his folded hands in his lord's hands. That showed that he served him.
24957.m: The vassal placed his hands in his lord's hands.

24958.q: What is the lord who grants a fief called?
24958.e: The liege lord passed land on to others. In return he demanded help in war.
24958.m: The liege lord grants the land.

24959.q: What could happen to a vassal who betrayed his lord?
a: He had to pay fewer dues
24959.e: Anyone who betrayed his lord was not allowed to keep the land. The lord could take the fief away from him.
24959.m: A vassal could lose his fief again.

24960.q: What did a vassal have to promise his liege lord?
24960.e: The vassal swore an oath of loyalty to his lord. He promised always to help him.
24960.m: The vassal promises his lord loyalty.

24961.q: Who received land from the king and passed land on to knights himself?
24961.e: Dukes and counts received large territories from the king. They granted parts of them to knights.
24961.m: A duke could receive fiefs and pass them on.

24962.q: Which other word is used for the system of fiefs?
24962.e: The word feudalism comes from the Latin “feudum”. That means fief.
24962.m: The system of fiefs is also called feudalism.

24963.q: Who worked the fields on the lords' land in the Middle Ages?
24963.e: The farmers worked in the fields. They had to give part of the harvest to the lord.

24965.q: In which two countries was Eleanor of Aquitaine queen?
24965.e: Eleanor first married the King of France. Her second husband became King of England shortly after the wedding.
24965.m: Eleanor was Queen of France and of England.

24966.q: Which famous king was the son of Eleanor of Aquitaine?
24966.e: Richard the Lionheart was Eleanor's favourite son. She often helped him to rule.
24966.m: Richard the Lionheart was Eleanor's son.

24967.e: Aquitaine is a region in south-west France. Eleanor inherited this large territory.

24968.q: Roughly how old did Eleanor of Aquitaine live to be?
24968.e: Eleanor died in 1204 at about 80. For the Middle Ages that was very old.

24969.q: Which great journey did Eleanor go on with her first husband?
24969.e: Eleanor went with the French king on the Second Crusade. She travelled all the way to the Holy Land.

24970.q: Which artists did Eleanor of Aquitaine like to bring to her court?
24970.e: Troubadours sang their songs at Eleanor's court. Troubadours were poets and singers.

24971.q: What did Eleanor collect a lot of money for when her son Richard was a prisoner?
24971.e: Richard the Lionheart was taken prisoner. Eleanor helped to collect the huge ransom so that he could go free.
24971.m: Eleanor helped to buy her son's freedom.

24972.q: Of which two countries was Eleanor of Aquitaine queen, one after the other?
24972.e: Eleanor first married the King of France and later the King of England. She was one of the most powerful women of the Middle Ages.
24972.m: Eleanor was Queen of France and of England.

24973.q: Of which country was Richard the Lionheart king?
24973.e: Richard was King of England from 1189. He reigned for ten years.
24973.m: Richard the Lionheart was King of England.

24974.q: Why was Richard nicknamed the Lionheart?
24974.e: Richard was seen as a very brave fighter. That is why people said he had the heart of a lion.

24975.q: Which military campaign to the Holy Land did Richard the Lionheart take part in?
24975.e: Richard fought in the Third Crusade in the Holy Land. But he could not capture Jerusalem.
24975.m: Richard fought in the Third Crusade.

24976.q: Who was Richard's great opponent in the Holy Land?
24976.e: Saladin was a sultan and ruler of Egypt and Syria. Richard and Saladin had great respect for each other.
24976.m: Saladin was Richard's opponent in the Holy Land.

24977.q: In which country was Richard taken prisoner on his way home?
24977.e: Duke Leopold of Austria took Richard prisoner in 1192. He locked him up in Dürnstein Castle on the Danube.
24977.m: Richard was taken prisoner in Austria.

24979.q: Which language did Richard the Lionheart mainly speak?
24979.e: Richard spent most of his life in France. He spoke French and probably hardly any English.

24980.q: In which famous story does King Richard often appear at the end?
24980.e: In many Robin Hood stories, King Richard comes back and rewards Robin Hood.
24980.m: King Richard appears in Robin Hood.

24981.q: What was the name of Richard's brother who became king after him?
24981.e: After Richard died in 1199, his brother John became king. He was called John Lackland.

24982.q: Which country did William the Conqueror conquer?
24982.e: William came across the sea with an army. He defeated the English king and became King of England himself.

24983.q: In which year did William conquer England?
24983.e: The conquest of England took place in 1066. It is one of the best-known years in English history.

24984.q: At which famous battle was William the Conqueror victorious?
24984.e: William defeated the English at the Battle of Hastings. After that he was able to conquer England.

24985.q: What was the name of the English king William defeated?
24985.e: King Harold fell in the Battle of Hastings. That is how William became king.

24986.q: Where did William the Conqueror come from?
24986.e: William was Duke of Normandy. Normandy is in the north of France.

24987.q: Across which sea did William sail with his ships to England?
24987.e: The English Channel lies between France and England. William brought his army and many horses across by ship.

24988.q: Which famous tower did William have built in London?
24988.e: William had a strong stone castle built in London. Its oldest part is called the White Tower.
24988.m: William built the Tower of London.

24989.q: What did William the Conqueror have counted and written down all over England?
24989.e: In 1086, William had land, people and animals counted. That way he knew how much in dues he could demand.
24989.m: William had everything people owned in England written down.

24990.q: What is the big book in which William had everything owned in England written down called?
24990.e: In 1086, William had land, people and animals counted. It is all in the Domesday Book.
24990.m: The Domesday Book records what there was in England.

24991.q: What does the Bayeux Tapestry show?
24991.e: The tapestry tells in pictures how William conquered England. It also shows the Battle of Hastings.
24991.m: The Bayeux Tapestry shows the conquest of England.

24992.q: Roughly how long is the Bayeux Tapestry?
24992.e: The tapestry is almost 70 metres long. That is about as long as a row of 15 cars.
24992.m: The Bayeux Tapestry is almost 70 metres long.

24993.q: Roughly how tall is the Bayeux Tapestry?
24993.e: The tapestry is very long but only about 50 centimetres tall. So it is a narrow strip of pictures.
24993.m: The Bayeux Tapestry is only about half a metre tall.

24994.q: How were the pictures on the Bayeux Tapestry made?
24994.e: In fact the tapestry is an embroidery. The pictures were stitched onto linen cloth with woollen threads.

24995.q: Which star with a tail can be seen on the Bayeux Tapestry?
24995.e: In the year of the conquest, Halley's Comet was in the sky. People thought it was a sign, so it was embroidered.
24995.m: A comet can be seen on the Bayeux Tapestry.

24996.q: In which language are the words on the Bayeux Tapestry written?
24996.e: There are short texts in Latin above the pictures. Latin was the written language of the Middle Ages.
24996.m: The texts on the tapestry are in Latin.

24997.q: Which animals can you see especially often on the Bayeux Tapestry?
24997.e: The knights fought on horseback. That is why a great many horses are embroidered on the tapestry.
24997.m: There are many horses on the Bayeux Tapestry.

24998.q: How is the Bayeux Tapestry laid out?
a: Like a long strip of pictures
24998.e: The pictures follow one after another like in a comic. That way they tell the story from left to right.
24998.m: The tapestry tells its story like a comic.

24999.q: Which country did Joan of Arc come from?
24999.e: Joan of Arc was born around 1412 in the village of Domrémy in France.
24999.m: Joan of Arc came from France.

25000.q: Who did Joan of Arc fight against?
25000.e: Joan lived during the Hundred Years' War. She helped the French against the English.
25000.m: Joan of Arc fought against the English.

25001.q: Which city did Joan of Arc free in 1429?
25001.e: Joan helped to free the besieged city of Orléans. That is why she is also called the Maid of Orléans.

25002.q: What was Joan of Arc before she went to war?
25002.e: Joan was a farmer's daughter. She could not read or write.
25002.m: Joan of Arc was a farm girl.

25003.q: What did Joan of Arc say she heard?
25003.e: Joan said that saints had spoken to her. The voices had told her to help France.

25004.q: What did Joan of Arc wear in battle?
25004.e: Joan wore men's clothing and armour. She rode ahead of the soldiers with a banner.

25005.q: Which king did Joan of Arc take to Reims to be crowned?
25005.e: Joan went with Charles VII to Reims. There he was crowned King of France in 1429.
25005.m: Joan took Charles VII to be crowned.

25006.q: Roughly how old was Joan of Arc when she died?
25006.e: Joan was captured and burned in Rouen in 1431. She was only about 19 years old.
25006.m: Joan of Arc died very young.

25007.q: What is Joan of Arc in the Catholic Church today?
25007.e: Joan of Arc was declared a saint in 1920. She is a patron saint of France.
25007.m: Joan of Arc is a saint.

25008.q: What does the name Barbarossa mean?
25008.e: Barbarossa is Italian and means “red beard”. Frederick had a reddish beard.

25009.e: Frederick became king in 1152 and emperor in Rome in 1155. He ruled the Holy Roman Empire.

25010.q: Which country did Barbarossa march into several times with his army?
25010.e: Barbarossa went to Italy six times. He wanted to rule the rich cities there.

25011.e: On a crusade in 1190, Barbarossa drowned in the River Saleph. It is in what is now Turkey.

25012.q: According to an old legend, in which mountain in Germany does Barbarossa sleep?
25012.e: According to the legend, Barbarossa sleeps in the Kyffhäuser. One day he is supposed to wake up and save his empire.
25012.m: According to legend, Barbarossa sleeps in the Kyffhäuser.

25013.q: According to the legend, what grows through the table where Barbarossa sleeps?
25013.e: The legend says that his beard has grown through the stone table. He has been asleep for a very long time.
25013.m: Barbarossa's beard grows through the table.

25014.q: Which ruling family did Frederick Barbarossa belong to?
25014.e: Barbarossa was a Hohenstaufen. The Hohenstaufen were a powerful family from Swabia.

25015.q: According to the legend, which birds fly around the mountain where Barbarossa sleeps?
25015.e: In the legend, Barbarossa sends a dwarf outside. As long as ravens still fly around the mountain, he must sleep on.
25015.m: In the Barbarossa legend, ravens fly around the mountain.

25016.q: In which country was Magna Carta written?
25016.e: Magna Carta was written in England in the Middle Ages. It is one of the most famous documents in the world.

25017.q: In which year was Magna Carta written?
25017.e: In June 1215, the English king had to agree to Magna Carta.

25018.e: Magna Carta is Latin. “Magna” means great and “Carta” means charter.

25019.q: Which king had to accept Magna Carta?
25019.e: King John Lackland had many quarrels with powerful nobles. They forced him to accept Magna Carta.

25020.q: Who forced the king to accept Magna Carta?
25020.e: The barons were powerful nobles. They were unhappy with the king and made demands.
25020.m: The barons pushed Magna Carta through.

a: A charter that limited the English king's power
The crown of the English kings
25021.e: In Magna Carta of 1215, the king had to guarantee rights to the nobles. The king was also supposed to obey the law.
25021.m: Magna Carta limited the king's power.

25022.q: How did the king confirm Magna Carta?
25022.e: The king pressed his wax seal onto the charter. That made it valid.

25023.q: Which river is the meadow of Runnymede on, where Magna Carta was accepted?
25023.e: Runnymede is a meadow on the Thames west of London. Magna Carta was sealed there in June 1215.
25023.m: Magna Carta was accepted on the Thames.

25025.q: Apart from the sail, what else powered a longship?
25025.e: When no wind was blowing, the men rowed. That way the ship still moved forward.
25025.m: Without wind, the Vikings rowed their ship.

25026.q: What material did the Vikings build their ships from?
25026.e: The ships were built of wood, often oak. The planks were joined with iron rivets.
25026.m: Viking ships were built of wood.

25027.q: How many sails did a Viking longship have?
25027.e: A longship had one mast with a big square sail. It also had oars.
25027.m: A longship had one big square sail.

25028.q: Why could longships also sail on rivers?
a: They sat low and flat in the water
25028.e: Longships only reached a little way down into the water. That is why they could get into shallow rivers and onto beaches.
25028.m: Longships sat shallow in the water and could sail on rivers too.

25029.q: Where on the ship did the Vikings often hang their shields?
a: On the side of the ship
25029.e: The round shields were fixed in a row along the side of the ship. You can see this in many pictures.
25029.m: The shields hung in a row along the side of the ship.

25030.q: What was the Vikings' broad trading ship called?
25030.e: The knarr was broader than a longship. It had lots of room for goods and animals.
25030.m: The Vikings carried their goods in the knarr.

25031.q: In which country is the Viking Ship Museum in Roskilde?
25031.e: In Roskilde in Denmark you can see real Viking ships. They were recovered from the fjord.
25031.m: There are real Viking ships in Roskilde in Denmark.

25032.e: Runes are the written characters of the Germanic peoples. The Vikings also wrote with runes.
25032.m: Runes are ancient written characters of the Germanic peoples.

25033.q: What is the row of runes, named after its first characters, called?
25033.e: The first runes stand for the sounds F, U, Th, A, R and K. That is why the row is called futhark.
25033.m: The row of runes is called futhark, after its first characters.

25034.q: Why do runes have almost only straight lines?
a: They were easy to carve that way
25034.e: Runes were carved into wood, stone or bone. Straight lines are much easier to carve than curves.
25034.m: Runes have straight lines because they were carved.

25035.q: What are large stones with rune inscriptions called?
25035.e: Rune stones are often in memory of people who have died. There are especially many in Sweden.
25035.m: Rune stones are stones with carved runes.

25036.q: Which people from the north wrote with runes?
25036.e: The Vikings carved runes into wood, bone and stone. The Romans, on the other hand, wrote with Latin letters.

25037.q: Which peoples used to use runes as their writing?
25037.e: Runes are the ancient written characters of the Germanic peoples. They were carved into wood, stone or metal.
25037.m: Runes were the writing of the Germanic peoples.

25038.q: According to an old legend, which god found the runes?
25038.e: A Norse legend tells that Odin found the runes. For this he hung on a tree for nine nights.
25038.m: According to legend, Odin found the runes.

25039.q: Which Danish king had a large rune stone put up in Jelling?
25039.e: Harald Bluetooth had a large rune stone put up in Jelling. It says that he made the Danes Christian.
25039.m: Harald Bluetooth had a rune stone put up in Jelling.

25040.q: Which Viking was probably the first European to reach America?
25040.e: Leif Erikson sailed to North America. The sagas from Iceland tell of it.
25040.m: Leif Erikson was probably the first European to reach America.

25041.q: Who did the Vikings meet in North America around the year 1000?
25041.e: People had already lived in North America for a long time. The Vikings traded with them, but also fought against them.
25041.m: The Vikings met native peoples in America.

25042.q: What did Leif Erikson call the land he found in America?
25042.e: Leif called the land Vinland. The name probably means wine land, because according to the saga wild grapes grew there.
25042.m: Leif Erikson called the new land Vinland.

25043.q: In which present-day country were the remains of a Viking village in America found?
25043.e: Remains of Viking houses were found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. Newfoundland is part of Canada.
25043.m: Remains of a Viking village are in Canada.

25044.q: Roughly how many years before Columbus was Leif Erikson in America?
25044.e: Leif came around the year 1000, Columbus in 1492. That is a difference of about 500 years.
25044.m: Leif Erikson was in America about 500 years before Columbus.

25045.q: From which island did Leif Erikson sail to America?
25045.e: Leif lived with his family in Greenland. From there he sailed west as far as America.
25045.m: Leif Erikson started his journey in Greenland.

25047.q: What does the name Eriksson mean?
25047.e: The Vikings often added “son” to the father's name. So Eriksson means son of Erik.

25048.q: Which son of Erik the Red sailed as far as North America?
25048.e: Leif Erikson, the son of Erik the Red, reached North America around the year 1000. That was about 500 years before Columbus.
25048.m: Leif Erikson reached North America as early as around 1000.

25049.q: Why was Erik probably called “the Red”?
25049.e: Erik probably got his nickname because of his red hair and red beard.
25049.m: Erik the Red probably had red hair.

25050.q: Why did Erik the Red give the big island the name “Green land”?
a: Because the sea there was green
Because there were green stones there
25050.e: The saga says Erik chose an attractive name. That way he wanted to persuade lots of people to come with him. This became the name Greenland.
25050.m: With the name Greenland, Erik wanted to attract settlers.

25051.q: From which island was Erik the Red banished before he sailed to Greenland?
25051.e: Erik first lived in Iceland. After a quarrel in which people died, he had to leave the island for a few years.
25051.m: Erik the Red was banished from Iceland.

25052.q: Which big island did Erik the Red explore and settle?
25052.e: Around 982, Erik the Red explored the coast of Greenland. Then he came back with settlers.

25053.q: In which country was Erik the Red born?
25053.e: Erik was born in Norway. As a child he came to Iceland with his father.
25053.m: Erik the Red came from Norway.

25054.q: Roughly when did Erik the Red found the settlements in Greenland?
25054.e: Around the year 985, Erik sailed to Greenland with many ships and settlers. There they set up farms.
25054.m: Erik the Red founded settlements in Greenland around 985.

25055.q: How did the first settlers get to Iceland?
a: On foot over a land bridge
25055.e: Iceland is an island far out in the sea. The settlers came in Viking ships more than 1000 years ago.
25055.m: The settlers came to Iceland by ship.

25056.q: Which country did most of the settlers in Iceland come from?
25056.e: Most settlers came from Norway. Some also came from the British Isles.
25056.m: Most of Iceland's settlers came from Norway.

25057.q: Who settled Iceland more than 1000 years ago?
25057.e: Vikings from Norway sailed to Iceland in their ships. They built farms there and stayed.

25059.q: What does the name Reykjavík mean?
25059.e: The settlers saw steam rising from hot springs there. They thought it was smoke and called the place smoky bay.

25060.q: What is the assembly founded in Iceland around 930 called?
25060.e: In 930 the Icelanders met for the first Althing. There they made laws and settled disputes.
25060.m: The Althing in Iceland was founded around 930.

25061.q: Which small horse did the settlers bring with them to Iceland?
25061.e: The settlers brought their horses with them on ships. They became the Icelandic horse, which still lives there today.
25061.m: The Icelandic horse came to Iceland with the settlers.

25062.q: Who sometimes lived in Iceland even before the Vikings?
25062.e: Old reports tell of Irish monks in Iceland. They went there to find peace for praying.
25062.m: Irish monks lived in Iceland before the Vikings.

25063.e: Hedeby was one of the most important Viking trading places. Merchants from many countries met there.
25063.m: Hedeby was a big Viking trading place.

25064.q: In which present-day country is Hedeby?
25064.e: Hedeby is in Schleswig-Holstein in the north of Germany. At that time the area belonged to Denmark.
25064.m: Hedeby is in the north of Germany today.

25065.q: What did the people of Hedeby live in?
25065.e: The houses in Hedeby were made of wood and had roofs of reed or straw. Some have been rebuilt for the museum.
25065.m: In Hedeby people lived in wooden houses.

25066.q: What protected the settlement of Hedeby on the land side?
25066.e: A big semicircular rampart surrounded Hedeby. It protected the houses from attacks.

25067.q: Which metal did the merchants in Hedeby often pay with?
25067.e: The merchants often paid with silver. Coins and jewellery were even cut into pieces for this.
25067.m: In Hedeby people often paid with silver.

25068.q: How did the merchants in Hedeby check how much silver they were getting?
25068.e: With silver, it was the weight that counted. That is why merchants carried small folding scales with weights.
25068.m: The merchants weighed the silver on scales.

25069.q: Which sea was Hedeby connected to by a long inlet?
25069.e: Hedeby lies on the Schlei, a long inlet of the Baltic Sea. That made it easy for ships to land.
25069.m: Hedeby was on an inlet of the Baltic Sea.

25071.q: An almost complete Viking helmet, the Gjermundbu helmet, was found in Norway. Roughly how old is it?
25071.e: The helmet dates from the 10th century, so from the Viking Age. It is about a thousand years old.
25071.m: The Gjermundbu helmet is about a thousand years old.

25072.q: How did horned helmets become famous for Vikings in the 19th century?
25072.e: Real Viking helmets had no horns. For Richard Wagner's operas in 1876, helmets with horns were designed, and that is how the false picture became well known.
25072.m: Horned helmets come from the costumes of an opera.

25073.q: What material were real Viking helmets made of?
25073.e: The few helmets that have been found are made of iron. Iron protected the head well.
25073.m: Real Viking helmets were made of iron.

25074.q: How many almost complete Viking helmets are known so far?
25074.e: Only very few almost complete Viking helmets are known, otherwise mostly small fragments. The best known is the Gjermundbu helmet.
25074.m: Only very few almost complete Viking helmets have been found.

25075.q: In which country was the Gjermundbu helmet found?
25075.e: The helmet was discovered in a grave on a farm in Norway in 1943.
25075.m: The Gjermundbu helmet was found in Norway.

25076.q: What does the Gjermundbu helmet have in front of the eyes?
a: A guard like a pair of glasses
25076.e: The helmet has a metal guard at the front for the eyes and nose. It looks a bit like a pair of glasses.
25076.m: The Gjermundbu helmet has an eye guard like glasses.

25077.q: What shape were Viking helmets usually at the top?
25077.e: The helmets had a round cap. That made blows slide off the head more easily.
25077.m: Viking helmets were round at the top.

25078.q: Who is the father of the gods for the Vikings?
25078.e: Odin is the highest god in the Norse legends. He is seen as wise and clever.
25078.m: Odin is the father of the Viking gods.

25079.e: Thor's hammer is called Mjölnir. According to legend, it comes back to Thor's hand after every throw.

25080.q: Thor is the god of which weather?
25080.e: Thor is the thunder god. The Vikings believed his hammer made lightning and thunder.
25080.m: Thor is the god of thunder.

25081.q: How many eyes does Odin have in the legends?
25081.e: Odin gave up an eye to drink from a spring of wisdom. That is why he only has one eye left.
